question: On 26 September 2025, the EU Ambassador to Libya announced that Operation IRINI had provided training to 30 maritime officials, of whom 15 were from eastern Libya, in Taranto, Sicily. In its response to written question E-004025/20251, the Commission refers to them as members of the ‘eastern branch of the LCG’ [Libyan coast guard].

In fact, Benghazicontrolled eastern Libya has no state coast guard under civilian ministerial supervision, as there exists in Tripoli in the west. The sea is instead patrolled by militias such as the Tariq bin Sijad Brigade, which is subordinate to the Libyan National Army (LNA), a body not recognised by the EU.
The LNA has been implicated in war crimes and crimes against humanity, and linked to the sanctioned Wagner Group. 1.
From which specific militia or non-state armed group did the 15 trainees recruited in Benghazi come, and under whose command structure do they operate?
How does the Commission justify training members of forces controlled by the LNA, even though it is not recognised by either the EU or the UN and cooperates with sanctioned actors?

Is the Commission certain that the individuals trained in eastern Libya have not been implicated in war crimes, human rights violations or illegal push-back operations, and what oversight arrangements are used to ensure this?
answer: EN E-00334/2026 on behalf of the European Commission (14.4.2026) 1. The 15 trainees from Benghazi who attended the course in Taranto last September were officers and petty officers from the Libyan Coast Guard part of the Libyan Navy, which is the sole Libyan military institution operating as a unified entity at operational level, under the umbrella of the Joint Military Committee. 2.

The EU engages with authorities throughout the country in line with its ‘one Libya’ policy and in accordance with the UN Security Council, which ‘noted the importance of progress towards the unification of all institutions, including military and security institutions’1. 3. All reasonable measures to mitigate such risks have been taken.

Every candidate is subject to a vetting process which involves an initial screening by Libyan authorities, followed by further checks by Member States, International Criminal Police Organisation (Interpol) and EU Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) prior to the start of the training.
EU Naval Force Mediterranean Operation Irini (EUNAVFOR MED IRINI) does not train personnel belonging to militias, nor individuals with a proven criminal record or a record of human rights violations.
